clue.text: Had a droll novel? He had several!

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new or freshly made, so these letters are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a funny novel was written, and the reply is that this writer produced many.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' seems to be the thing he wrote, but it is the anagram signal working on HAD A DROLL; the exclamation 'He had several!' then defines the author by his many novels.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh-born children's author wrote many books, so he certainly had several novels to his name.

clue.text: Jason going to steal finds a way to Colchis at last

parts.note: to steal is to rob
RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

indicators.note: at last picks the final letter of the word Colchis

explanation.surface: The mythical Jason, out to steal the Golden Fleece, finds a route to Colchis.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is Jason and the Argonauts, but the Jason meant is the American actor Jason Robards.
explanation.definitionFit: Jason is the first name of the American stage and film actor surnamed Robards, a forename-for-surname clue.

clue.text: Huxley's caper on grass?

parts.note: Aldous Huxley's novel title pairs a word for a caper or prank with a word for dried grass; the clue asks for the caper word

explanation.surface: A question about some playful antics by Huxley out on the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Huxley's 1923 novel is Antic Hay: the answer means a caper, and hay is dried grass, so the caper is literally 'on grass' in the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful caper or grotesque bit of clowning is called by this word, which opens the title of Huxley's novel.

clue.text: Jules et Jim, say, in a work by Colette

definitions.meaning: the two friends of Truffaut's film are an example of a pair
Colette published a short novel of this title in 1934

explanation.definitionFit: Jules and Jim are a pair, and Colette's 1934 novel bears this title too.

clue.text: What Rita thought was getting the rhyme wrong

definitions.text: What Rita thought was getting the rhyme wrong

parts.words: What Rita thought was getting the rhyme wrong
parts.note: in Willy Russell's play Educating Rita, the heroine defines a poetic term for echoed vowel sounds as getting the rhyme wrong

explanation.surface: A student's naive idea of a poetic device as a botched rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: In Educating Rita, Rita's answer for this term is that it means 'getting the rhyme wrong', a line that wins her tutor over.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names the echo of vowel sounds without full rhyme, which Rita aptly calls getting the rhyme wrong.

clue.text: The flower of French thieves

parts.note: the reading combines a garden plant name with the finest of French thieves, Arsène, Maurice Leblanc's gentleman burglar

explanation.surface: Praise for the pick of France's criminal class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' means the finest of a group, and Arsène of that surname is Maurice Leblanc's gentleman thief; it is also a garden plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a tall garden plant with spikes of blooms and Leblanc's famous French gentleman burglar.

clue.text: Least complicated one's were unexpected

indicators.note: complicated means tangled or mixed up, so the letters of the word least are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone notes that even the simplest stories were full of surprises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' is 1 Across, the author: his television series was Tales of the Unexpected.
explanation.definitionFit: The author's short stories, televised as a series of the Unexpected, are his stories of that kind.

clue.text: After time I locate her broadcast — it's speculative

indicators.note: after means the rearranged letters follow the time letter in the answer
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of I locate her are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tracks down a woman after a while, though the claim is only a guess.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hypothetical rather than proven is speculative.

clue.text: Supposed author of Salmagundi, a Queen's lover going about University

indicators.note: going about means the knight's name surrounds the university letter

parts.note: Sir Lancelot was the lover of Queen Guinevere in Arthurian legend

explanation.surface: An Arthurian knight is pictured hanging about a university, credited with a literary periodical.
explanation.walkthrough: Salmagundi (1807) was Washington Irving's satirical periodical, attributed in jest to Launcelot Langstaff.
explanation.definitionFit: Irving's periodical pretended to be written by a fictional gentleman, Langstaff, whose first name is this.

clue.text: A Bogart movie has attraction to mostly transport one

parts.note: SA is short for sex appeal, an attraction

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter of the word for transport is dropped

parts.note: to bring is to transport or carry along
A means one, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: A Bogart film is said to have the pull to carry a viewer away.
explanation.walkthrough: SA (sex appeal) is a crossword staple; 'mostly' trims BRING to BRIN. The 1954 film stars Humphrey Bogart and Audrey Hepburn.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1954 Billy Wilder romantic comedy starring Humphrey Bogart carries this title.

clue.text: It's mechanical to drink your good health

definitions.text: It's mechanical to drink your good health

parts.words: It's mechanical to drink your good health
parts.note: the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream is one of the rude mechanicals; his name with 's makes a drinking toast

explanation.surface: A remark that toasting someone's health has become a reflex.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'rude mechanicals' are the amateur actors in A Midsummer Night's Dream; the weaver among them gives the toast its first word.
explanation.definitionFit: The toast urging everyone to drain their glasses is a cheerful call to drink to someone's health.

clue.text: Part of town, Abraham's birthplace, mentioned in old book

indicators.note: in means the city's name goes inside the letters for old book

parts.note: EX means former or old, as in ex-wife
Ur of the Chaldees is named in Genesis as the patriarch's home city

explanation.surface: Abraham's home city is said to appear in an ancient scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: A prosperous district beyond the suburbs is an outlying area, a part of a town's spread.

clue.text: French narrative set in Nanterre city

indicators.note: set in means the answer is lodged within the words Nanterre city

explanation.surface: A French story is located in the town of Nanterre.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for an account or story is used in English for a narrative, especially in music or literature.

clue.text: Operetta, including one in a du Maurier novel depicted on a panel

indicators.note: on means in this down clue the first part sits above the next
in means the single letter goes inside the novel's title

parts.note: Trilby (1894) is George du Maurier's novel about the hypnotist Svengali
A means one, a single item
a jury is a panel of people chosen to give a verdict

explanation.surface: An operetta incorporating a character from a du Maurier novel is painted on a panel.
explanation.walkthrough: The novel is Trilby by George du Maurier, not his granddaughter Daphne; the operetta is Gilbert and Sullivan's.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert and Sullivan's one-act comic opera of 1875 is this courtroom piece.

clue.text: Author of Sleep, Canadian's latest ironic novel about something imaginary

indicators.note: latest picks the final letter of the word Canadian's
novel means new, so the letters of ironic take a fresh order

parts.note: C is short for circa, about
i is the imaginary unit in mathematics, the square root of minus one

explanation.surface: A Canadian writer's latest novel is ironic and concerns something unreal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like the book, but it is the anagram signal: IRONIC becomes INORIC. The author is himself Canadian, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: The Canadian novelist wrote Sleep (2015), so he is its author.

clue.text: Quiet like Bird or like a playwright

parts.note: SH is the call for quiet
avian means like a bird

explanation.surface: A question of whether something is quiet like a bird or in the manner of a dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: The playwright is George Bernard Shaw; the adjective from his name describes his style.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything in the manner of George Bernard Shaw, the Irish dramatist.

clue.text: "To triumph like an — trull / Upon their woes" (Henry VI, Part 3)

definitions.text: "To triumph like an — trull / Upon their woes" (Henry VI, Part 3)

parts.words: "To triumph like an — trull / Upon their woes" (Henry VI, Part 3)
parts.note: York taunts Queen Margaret for gloating like a warrior woman of legend; the missing word is the adjective for those women

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: York's speech to Margaret compares her to a female warrior of Greek legend; the gap is the adjective for those warriors.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective describes a warlike woman, like the female fighters of Greek myth.

clue.text: A daughter drunk in the morning over a precocious child

indicators.note: over means the whole string of pieces is turned back to front

parts.note: lit is slang for drunk
AM stands for ante meridiem, in the morning

explanation.surface: A daughter tipsy in the morning, all over a gifted youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses all of A, D, LIT, AM together. The child is the heroine of the Dahl novel, fitting the 1 Across theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahl's heroine is a little girl of startling cleverness, a precocious child.

clue.text: David's stepfather, having knocked back liquor gets dead drunk mostly

indicators.note: knocked back suggests the drink word is turned around

parts.note: rum is a liquor
D is an abbreviation for dead, as in genealogies

indicators.note: mostly means the final letter of the word for drunk is dropped

parts.note: stoned is slang for drunk or intoxicated

explanation.surface: A stepfather who has knocked back his spirits and is nearly legless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' reads as downing a drink but turns RUM into MUR; STONED loses its last letter. The stepfather is from Dickens's David Copperfield.
explanation.definitionFit: In Dickens's David Copperfield, the cruel Edward of this name marries David's mother.

clue.text: Vintage consumed in Corfu from time to time

indicators.note: from time to time picks every other letter of Corfu, starting with the first

explanation.surface: A vintage wine drunk now and then on the island of Corfu.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a growth of wine names a vineyard or class of vintage.

clue.text: Bucket that's seen by Mrs Mop at front of launderette

parts.note: a char is a cleaning lady, nicknamed Mrs Mop in British slang

indicators.note: front of picks the first letter of the word launderette

parts.note: IE stands for id est, that is

explanation.surface: A bucket is spotted beside a cleaning lady in front of a laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bucket' looks like a cleaner's pail, but it is the surname of Dahl's boy in Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. A char, nicknamed Mrs Mop, is a British cleaning woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahl's hero of the chocolate factory story is a boy surnamed Bucket.

clue.text: Clown's joke about one in a play

indicators.note: about means the joke word goes around the player

parts.note: cod as a noun means a hoax or joke
a star is a leading actor in a play

explanation.surface: A clown cracks a joke about a member of the cast.
explanation.walkthrough: The clown is from Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's rustic jester in Love's Labour's Lost bears this name.

clue.text: Conrad, storyteller about Switzerland, not featuring women

indicators.note: about means the trimmed storyteller goes around the country letters
not featuring means the letter for women is left out

parts.note: a writer tells stories
CH is the international code for Switzerland, Confoederatio Helvetica

explanation.surface: Joseph Conrad is cast as a teller of tales about Switzerland that leave women out.
explanation.walkthrough: Conrad suggests Joseph Conrad, but the writer meant is the American novelist Conrad Richter, author of The Town.
explanation.definitionFit: Conrad is the forename of the American Pulitzer-winning novelist surnamed Richter.

clue.text: Travers's nook where plants can be grown, partly open rather than partly closed

indicators.text: partly open rather than partly closed
indicators.note: the first letter of open replaces the first letter of closed in the garden word

parts.note: a rockery is a garden of stones where plants grow

explanation.surface: A garden corner for plants, opened up rather than shut.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Travers wrote the 1926 farce Rookery Nook; the answer is its first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Travers's Aldwych farce is titled after a country house called Rookery Nook.

clue.text: Birds like Hedwig to cry out in falls

indicators.note: in means the cry is placed inside the word for falls

parts.note: snows falls from the sky as snow
to yowl is to cry out loudly

explanation.surface: Harry Potter's owl is told to screech in the waterfalls.
explanation.walkthrough: Hedwig is Harry Potter's white owl.
explanation.definitionFit: Hedwig, Harry Potter's pet, is a white Arctic owl species, so these birds are like her.

clue.text: In which female group's about to include leader of coven?

definitions.text: In which female group's about to include leader of coven?

parts.note: WI is the Women's Institute, a British women's organisation

indicators.note: to include means the about letters go around the coven's leader

parts.note: CA is short for circa, about

indicators.note: leader of picks the first letter of the word coven

explanation.surface: A women's group is about to take in a witches' coven leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute (WI) is a British organisation of women; the whole clue also defines the answer, a religion whose practitioners meet in covens.
explanation.definitionFit: The modern pagan witchcraft religion is practised in covens, often with female leadership.

clue.text: Miss Lenya losing energy for nothing on which you'd gamble

indicators.note: the letter for energy is dropped and replaced by a zero-shaped letter for nothing

parts.note: Lotte Lenya was the Austrian singer and actress

explanation.surface: The singer Lotte Lenya runs out of energy for no reason.
explanation.walkthrough: E is energy in physics; O, a zero, means nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The lottery game is something you stake money on, a form of gambling.

clue.text: One's practical jokers take turns shunning society

indicators.note: shunning means the letter for society is avoided and removed

parts.note: twists means turns, as in a road's twists

explanation.surface: Pranksters take turns avoiding company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is 1 Across: in Dahl's The Twits, Mr and Mrs Twit play nasty tricks on each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahl's grubby couple spend the book playing cruel tricks on each other, so they are his pranksters.

clue.text: A Farewell to Arms initially admired occasionally by upper-class

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word Arms
occasionally picks every other letter of admired, starting from the second

parts.note: U means upper-class in British usage

explanation.surface: Hemingway's novel is admired now and then by the upper classes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface borrows Hemingway's title A Farewell to Arms; the definition is only 'A Farewell'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for goodbye is used in English as a farewell.

clue.text: What'll make you recoil catching fish? According to one, it's enormous

indicators.note: catching means the word recoil holds the fish inside it
what will make the answer tells us the letters are reworked into it

parts.note: cod is a fish

explanation.surface: Something that makes you flinch catches fish and is reckoned huge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' is 1 Across: Dahl wrote The Enormous Crocodile. RECOIL catching COD gives RECOCODIL, which is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahl's picture book is titled The Enormous Crocodile, so to him the reptile is enormous.

clue.text: Uplifting work, one of Eliot's

definitions.meaning: a lyric poem of praise elevates its subject
T. S. Eliot published a poem with this title in 1920

explanation.definitionFit: A lyric poem of exalted praise is uplifting, and T. S. Eliot wrote one titled so.

clue.text: Damsel in distress primarily with yen for one's champion

indicators.note: in means the girl's name sits inside the other letters
primarily picks the first letter of the word distress

parts.note: Y is the symbol for the yen, Japan's currency
Ann is a girl's name, standing for a damsel

explanation.surface: A damsel in distress longs for a champion to rescue her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' is 1 Across: Dahl wrote Danny, the Champion of the World. ANN goes between D and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahl's novel names the boy as the Champion of the World, so he is that author's champion.

clue.text: "… they kiss / Briefly, -, imponderably" (Ted Hughes)

parts.note: a line from Ted Hughes with a gap filled by an adverb meaning timelessly

explanation.surface: A Ted Hughes quotation with a missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in a way untouched by time, which fits a brief yet timeless kiss.
